canberra.title: Elderly man with dementia murdered wife, but unfit to plead
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to family violence. An elderly man with dementia has been found to have murdered his wife, although ...
canberra.content:
Manfred Uhle killed his wife, Wanda Dorothy Uhle, at their Gordon home on 2 June 2024. Photo: Supplied.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to family violence.

An elderly man with dementia has been found to have murdered his wife, although he is also unfit to plead to his charge due to his mental health conditions.

Region has previously reported how Manfred Uhle did not think his wife of 60 years, Wanda Dorothy Uhle, was dead a year after he fatally stabbed her.

The ACT Supreme Court then found he was unfit to plead to his charge of murder in March 2026, partly as he had Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia and had been in cognitive decline since at least mid-2023.

This decision was legally suppressed at the time, preventing it from being reported.

But Justice Andrew Muller lifted this order on Friday (18 September) when also announcing he was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the 88-year-old’s actions had met each of the elements of the offence of murder.

Justice Muller said members of Mr Uhle’s family began noticing changes in 2021 as he had started becoming highly anxious and fearful, which was out of character. He later began experiencing episodes of confusion and memory loss.

Family members suggested Mr and Mrs Uhle engage with aged care services or assisted living arrangements, but neither of them accepted this assistance.

In the lead-up to the murder, his family also noticed he was having increasing episodes of paranoid and persecutory ideation.

Justice Muller said early in the morning of 2 June 2024, Mr Uhle took a 32 cm knife into the bedroom of their home in the southern Canberra suburb of Gordon, got into bed with Mrs Uhle and told her, “I’m going to kill you”.

He began to stab her while she tried to defend herself, and he continued as she ran through the house. She died in the doorway, aged 78, and an autopsy would later find she had 33 stab wounds.

Meanwhile, Mr Uhle left her body there and drove to his granddaughter’s home. She opened the door to find him covered in blood.

Police arrested him later that morning, and he has remained in custody ever since.

Justice Muller said Mr Uhle agreed he stabbed Mrs Uhle.

“[It] is beyond reasonable doubt that Mr Uhle stabbed his wife repeatedly with a knife, resulting in her death,” he said.

Prosecutors argued the only suitable order would be to remand Mr Uhle in custody for review by the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal (ACAT) under the Mental Health Act 2015.

“I indicated to the parties I would provide an opportunity for further submissions on that topic with a view to exploring whether there is a suitable alternative in Mr Uhle’s case that would see him released from custody to facilitate an ACAT assessment for the purpose of making a mental health order,” Justice Muller said.

The matter was adjourned to 7 October for submissions.

Anyone impacted by sexual, domestic or family violence can contact 1800RESPECT on 1800 737 732 or Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. Local support services include the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service (DVCS) on 6280 0900, and Victim Support ACT on 1800 822 272 or 6205 2022. If this reporting has raised mental health concerns for you, call Lifeline on 13 11 14.

canberra.title: ‘Daddy is watching over them’: Father-of-four’s fatal stabbing devastates family
canberra.snippet: There is now a tradition for the Cordingley family. Every time there is a clear night, his former partner takes their four sons outside t...
canberra.content:
The trial of Robert Mathew Marshall heard from many connected to the town of Marulan, near Goulburn. Photo: File.

There is now a tradition for the Cordingley family. Every time there is a clear night, his former partner takes their four sons outside their home and points out the brightest star in the sky.

“I tell them that Daddy is watching over them,” Adam Cordingley’s clearly emotional former partner, Kate, told the NSW Supreme Court on Friday (18 September).

She was speaking about the impact of Adam’s death after Robert Mathew Marshall was found guilty of killing the 38-year-old at the end of his jury trial.

The court heard Adam had been devastated when he learned Kate had a 12-month affair with Marshall that ended in mid-2023.

On the night of 23 March 2024, Marshall left the Terminus Hotel in Marulan, where he worked as a chef, then returned to his farm on Oallen Ford Road in Bungonia and found Adam on his property, wanting to speak about the affair.

A scuffle broke out between the two, during which Marshall used a hunting knife to stab Adam three times. A 14 to 18 cm deep cut to his hip went through bone before hitting an artery, resulting in his death.

At the end of the trial, jurors rejected the then-42-year-old’s claims of self-defence when finding him guilty of a charge of manslaughter, although clearing him of murder.

“My children lost a father. A father who was deeply involved in their lives,” Kate said during Marshall’s sentencing hearing on Friday.

Their home is now filled with photos of him, which Kate said helps remind the boys of the love he had for them.

“It is important for me to reassure the boys and help them understand their feelings are normal, and to strengthen their bond with Adam,” she said.

“We talk about Adam and remember the special moments we shared as a family, keeping those moments alive for the boys.”

Adam was also the second son lost to his parents, Julie and Ted Cordingley, as his older brother Glenn died after an accident years earlier.

Julie told the court losing two of their children was heartbreaking and unimaginable.

“It weighs heavily on our minds knowing that Adam was so unhappy and he died alone with only the perpetrator present,” she said.

“It’s often in the quiet moments that the pain of losing Adam feels especially intense.

“The sadness and grief can be overwhelming, and the tears flow as we remember how much he meant to us.”

Julie said Adam was proud of his sons and it had been wonderful to see him so happy around them. She also said Kate had continued to provide their children with a stable and supportive environment since his death.

“We will always remember Adam and love him, and will watch over his boys, and he would hope us to do,” she said.

In a statement, Adam’s younger brother, Joel Cordingley, said they had been mates who planned to take over their family’s farm one day.

He is the godfather to Adam’s sons and loved them dearly, but “cannot replace their father”.

“The killing of Adam has devastated me. Every day I feel anger, sadness and heartbreak,” Joel said.

“Losing another brother in such violent circumstances has left wounds that will never fully heal.”

Kate also said she and Adam had been trying to work through the impact of her affair. She had been trying to move forward together and regain his trust.

“I genuinely wanted us to try and find a way forward and create a positive environment for our children,” she said.

She said she now tended to keep to herself, worried about being judged or misunderstood, and often felt lonely.

“I long for the comfort of familiar faces and understanding friends,” she said.

Prosecutor Nerissa Keay argued the court would be satisfied Marshall stabbed Adam with the intention of causing grievous bodily harm.

She said there was no dispute Marshall was a person of prior good character, that the circumstances he faced that night were difficult and he was unlikely to reoffend.

Marshall’s barrister, David Dalton SC, said his client had armed himself with the knife because he arrived home to find what he thought was an unknown intruder on his property.

He said after Marshall spoke to Adam, he tried to walk away, but was grabbed and swung around.

“This is a terrible and tragic mistake,” Mr Dalton said.

He also said his client, who is in custody, had repeatedly expressed remorse over Adam’s death, including on the night he died.

Justice Paul McGuire is expected to hand down his sentence on 25 September.

canberra.title: Planning tick paves way for Telopea Park High School expansion
canberra.snippet: Telopea Park High School’s $53.4 million expansion program is set to go ahead after Planning and Sustainable Development Minister C...
canberra.content:
What the Telopea Park High School extension may look like. Image: ACT Government.

Telopea Park High School’s $53.4 million expansion program is set to go ahead after Planning and Sustainable Development Minister Chris Steel approved the rezoning of a neighbouring block of land used as a playing field.

The Major Plan Amendment (MPA-10) will rezone Blocks 4 and 5, Section 36 Forrest and parts of the road reserve for New South Wales Crescent and Manuka Circle adjoining Blocks 4 and 5 from PRZ2 Restricted Access Recreation Zone to Community Facility Zone (CFZ).

Block 5 is the key piece of land. The rezoning will allow it to be used for “educational establishment uses”.

The ACT Government plans to expand the Senior Campus to provide more places and modern facilities to meet growing demand in the inner south.

The project will increase the school’s permanent capacity by 150 students and deliver a range of new facilities, including science labs, performing arts and music facilities, a new multipurpose hall and a double gymnasium.

Concept illustrations show a three-storey development, although the final design may differ as the project progresses.

The project will also include upgraded outdoor learning and recreation areas, landscaping and gardens, and 81 new parking spaces.

The new facilities will also be available for public use outside school hours. The tennis courts will be retained.

MPA-10 will need to pass the Legislative Assembly, but community consultation is underway in preparation for a development application.

Community consultation earlier in the year attracted 45 comments, mostly in support.

But concerns raised included the loss of green open space and the use of the oval for recreation and exercising dogs, traffic and parking issues, loss of amenity, privacy, and sunlight for nearby residents, and impacts on the character of the local area.

One change was made to MPA-10 after consultation. An environmental assessment report endorsed by the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) will be required.

Feedback is now being sought until 30 September from the school community, local residents, businesses and other interested stakeholders ahead of the DA being lodged.

Telopea Park School is a K-10, binational French Australian school whose catchment area includes the suburbs of Kingston, Red Hill, Griffith, Forrest, Barton, Narrabundah, Fyshwick, Beard, Symonston and Oaks Estate.

It is the designated public high school provider in this growing catchment for Years 7 to 10.

In 2023, the government decided against building a new high school in the Inner South to cater for population growth, opting instead to expand Telopea Park to eventually take 500 extra students.

The 2026 school census figures show an enrolment of 1056 for the high school years 7-10, making Telopea Park the biggest public high school in the ACT.

Overall, the school has 1595 students enrolled, with a capacity of 1784

canberra.title: Sports heroes tell public servants their stories of abuse at work
canberra.snippet: Public servants attending the Comcare conference in Canberra over the past week were given two stellar opportunities to hear from former ...
canberra.content:
AFL legend Adam Goodes in conversation with Virginia Trioli at the Comcare conference. Photo: Comcare.

Public servants attending the Comcare conference in Canberra over the past week were given two stellar opportunities to hear from former elite athletes sharing their experiences of abuse in the workplace.

AFL champion and former Australian of the Year, Adam Goodes, featured in a ‘fireside chat’ with broadcaster Virginia Trioli (the conference MC) at the conference dinner (15 September).

The next day, former World Number 4 Jelena Dokic addressed the audience.

With the conference theme being A people-first approach to workplace health and safety, their messages were powerful, pointed and relevant.

Goodes quit the AFL in 2015 after winning two Brownlow Medals, being a dual premiership player with his club, the Sydney Swans, and being named the 2014 Australian of the Year.

But his early retirement from the game followed years of racist abuse on the field, which eventually took its toll.

“Ninety-eight per cent of my working life as a footballer I was in a safe environment,” he told the Comcare crowd.

“I felt safe with my teammates, and the club I played for was very supportive.

“They were active in promoting inclusivity and making sure everyone respected each other.

“But for a couple of hours every week, playing the game in front of thousands of people, I was placed in what felt like a very unsafe environment for me and was subjected to all sorts of abuse.”

In the first match of the 2013 Indigenous round when the Swans were playing Collingwood, a 13-year-old girl Collingwood supporter yelled at Goodes, calling him an “ape”.

He pointed her out to security guards, and they escorted her from the ground.

The girl later rang to apologise to Goodes, and the footballer accepted it, publicly saying he didn’t blame the girl herself, but wanted to highlight how “shattering” the slur was.

He was constantly booed and racially abused at games after that incident, yet took every opportunity to speak out against racism in Australia.

In 2015, during the Swans’ Indigenous Round game against Carlton at the SCG, Goodes celebrated a goal by performing what some described as an Aboriginal war-cry dance and mimed throwing a spear at the Carlton supporters.

By the end of that season, Goodes had retired from the game, worn down by the abuse.

In June 2019, the AFL and its 18 clubs apologised unreservedly to Goodes for failing to support him adequately in the face of this abuse.

The AFL apology ended with: “We never want to see the mistakes of the past repeated.”

While Goodes acknowledged the apology, he did not return to the game, and devoted his time and influence to a wide range of Indigenous organisations.

“I was surprised at how much influence the AFL doesn’t have, or doesn’t want to have,” he said on Tuesday.

“Here’s an example. There was a teenage boy from a local club who started sending me pictures of monkeys and that kind of thing.

“I thought it would be good for him to maybe get some education about what he was actually doing and the impact of those kinds of actions, so I asked the AFL to maybe reach out to the kid and give him a lesson.

“They just came back saying they had no power to do anything at the local level and could only take action with actual AFL clubs.

“It seemed to me like they didn’t really get it. I think they could have done something. It’s at that level where minds and attitudes need to be shaped in the right direction.”

Former World No. 4 Jelena Dokic told her story at the Comcare conference. Photo: Comcare.

The Dokic story, also very public, played out even closer to home.

As a teenage rising tennis star, the abuse she copped – at work and at home – was from her own father.

Dokic pulled off one of tennis’s biggest upsets as a 16-year-old by beating then World Number 1 Martina Hingis in the first round of the 1999 Wimbledon Championships.

It was a decade earlier that her father showed up with a tennis racquet “that was bigger than me” after watching a match between Monica Seles and Steffi Graf at the 1989 French Open.

“Right after my very first tennis lesson, my father physically abused me,” Dokic said during her keynote address on Wednesday.

“My father’s abuse was made worse by his alcoholism and … by the time I was 11, I was hit with a leather belt constantly.

“There was mental abuse too … I was told ‘don’t you dare say anything. Don’t you dare say anything to anyone or I will kill you’.

“Those were the words I heard almost daily from my father. I was trained to be silent.”

Dokic’s journey with her father is well documented, not least because she managed to get away from the abuser.

“He was getting worse. He was unravelling. Some of his outbursts were becoming public,” she said.

“I decided to escape home at the age of 19, during a tournament, and run for my life.”

At 22, Dokic attempted suicide and by 29 she had ended her tennis career early.

Now a public speaker, author, broadcaster and tennis analyst, Dokic says her greatest achievement was finding her voice and telling her own story.

“That’s what saved my life,” she said.

“It’s been nine years since the day my first book came out, and it was the best day of my life.

“It saved my life. I really felt like I could start healing now.”

Dokic shared the three factors that made it all possible for her: people around her encouraged and helped her tell her story; she embraced the power of being vulnerable by sharing her story; and the support she’s received since she did.

canberra.title: Woman to be charged with killing two cyclists in fatal Gungahlin Drive crash
canberra.snippet: A woman will be charged with killing two cyclists after she allegedly drove a car into their group in northern Canberra last month. Bridi...
canberra.content:
18 September 2026

Join the conversation

1

A damaged car was spotted at the scene of the crash on Gungahlin Drive on 27 August 2026. Photo: John Lomnicki.

A woman will be charged with killing two cyclists after she allegedly drove a car into their group in northern Canberra last month.

Bridie Lee, Ryan Riethmuller and three other cyclists were riding on Gungahlin Drive in northern Canberra after 6 am on 27 August 2026 when a Hyundai Accent crashed into their group.

Tragically, 32-year-old Ms Lee died at the scene. Mr Riethmuller, 39, was taken to hospital, before he also died a week later.

A 34-year-old man had been treated at hospital before being released on the day of the crash.

The five cyclists had been riding as part of the Canberra Bilbys Triathlon Club’s regular cycling group that morning.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said officers from the Major Collision Team began an investigation before issuing the 40-year-old female driver with a summons on Friday (18 September).

She is expected to appear before the ACT Magistrates Court on 20 October to face two counts of culpable driving causing death and one count of negligent driving causing actual bodily harm.

australia.title: Australian man accused of murdering Thai teenager and putting body in suitcase pleads not guilty
australia.snippet: Simon Peter Carman appeared in a Pattaya court on Friday charged with killing Tunchanok Donhomla An Australian man accused of murdering a...
australia.content:
An Australian man accused of murdering a Thai teenager and putting her body in a suitcase pleaded not guilty on Friday in a hearing in the seaside resort city of Pattaya, a court official said.

Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested in June after 17-year-old Tunchanok Donhomla was reported missing in Pattaya City, about 150km south-east of Bangkok. A suitcase containing her body was found shortly after.

Police said she died of suffocation.

Carman appeared on Friday at Pattaya provincial court, where he pleaded not guilty to all charges, a court spokesperson said.

He had been charged with murder, concealing a body and taking a minor for indecent purposes. The next court date was set for 12 October.

Police previously said CCTV footage showed him entering a condominium in Pattaya with the girl in the early hours of 25 June, and leaving that evening carrying a large black suitcase.

In a police interrogation video shared online by Thai media, Carman has said he was acting in self-defence because the girl was threatening him with a knife.

The case put the spotlight on Pattaya, which is popular with foreign tourists for its beaches and nightlife, but also has a reputation for sex tourism.

australia.title: Swimmer dies after being bitten by shark off popular Perth beach
australia.snippet: Locals describe their shock at witnessing the incident at Sorrento Beach on Friday morning Follow our Australia news live blog for latest...
australia.content:
A man has died after being bitten by a shark off Sorrento Beach in Perth’s north.

Emergency services were called to the popular beach at about 10.30am on Friday after reports of a shark-related incident.

Western Australia police said a man had been bitten by a shark while swimming along the coast. He died as a result of his injuries, police said.

Emergency services, including water and air personnel, conducted an extensive search of the area. The swimmer’s body has not been found.

The Alkimos Surf Life Saving Club said Sorrento Beach will remain closed until 12pm on Saturday. Locals have been urged to stay out of the water until the beach was declared safe for swimming.

The City of Wanneroo has closed all other beaches along its coastline until 12pm on Saturday.

The local state MP, Liam Staltari, extended his condolences to the man’s family, friends and loved ones.

“Like all locals and people from across WA, I’m deeply saddened by the tragic death of a man following today’s shark attack at Sorrento Beach,” he said.

“Our entire community is thinking of you at this incredibly difficult time.”

A witness, Darrel Haythornthwaite, told 7News that he could not believe the incident had occurred, “especially in a place like this”. He said the man’s friend, who was swimming with him, made it back to shore but was inconsolable.

“He felt bad because he didn’t go back to save his mate and I said, ‘Nah you couldn’t have done that’,” he told the outlet. “There’s nothing that anyone could have done.”

Another witness, Ingrid Mitchell, told 9News she swam at the beach every day and did not expect sharks to attack outside of dawn and dusk.

“There was other swimmers in there … just near the seaweed, and there was one poor girl there who was sun-baking, and she saw the whole lot as well,” she said.

A third witness, Jacqui Rapaic, told the ABC she was walking along the beach with a friend when the incident occurred.

“My friend said, ‘Jac, I think there’s been a shark attack’ and I looked out to the ocean and I could see a pool of blood,” she said.

“I hugged onto my friend … [we] felt rather traumatised at that point. It happened so quickly.”

The fatality follows a shark attack on Monday at the remote Glenfield Beach, north of Geraldton on WA’s mid-west coast, which left a surfer with serious injuries.

He was taken to the nearby Geraldton health campus and is in a stable condition.

- with AAP

australia.title: Andrew Hastie says AI advised him to reply ‘congratulations!’ to man who planned to end life with assisted dying
australia.snippet: Liberal MP speaks of AI’s shortcomings as cyber chief tells inquiry the tech is needed to fend off ‘highly capable malicious cyber actors...
australia.content:
When a man with a terminal illness wrote to his local MP Andrew Hastie, telling him he planned on ending his own life with voluntary assisted dying, Microsoft Copilot suggested Hastie reply with “congratulations!”, “great to hear from you” or “that is wonderful news!”.

Hastie shared the episode at a parliamentary inquiry on Friday to underline the shortcomings of the American-run software as he called for AI run by Australians.

The hearing offered the some of the most detailed explanations of the Albanese government’s desire to bring Anthropic and OpenAI to Australia, in the face of calls to slow them down or shut them out.

The defence establishment told the inquiry that cutting the companies out could be catastrophic.

Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said her agents needed advanced AI every day to fend off “highly capable malicious cyber actors”.

“If a digital adversary has access to newer, more capable models than we do, they may be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in systems and networks before we can identify them,” Bradshaw said.

But Australia’s top cyber-intelligence agency is “entirely reliant” on US-housed processing and would “dramatically” lose capability if cut off in a conflict, Bradshaw said.

The defence department’s chief AI officer, Chris Crozier, said the government was already trying to keep its tech needs local, contracting Google to build a series of interlinked datacentres spread across the country and disconnected from the US.

“Somebody can’t wake up and have a bad day and decide they’re going to turn it off,” Crozier said.

“We do not want to be using AI tool sets that are located offshore … we want the compute, we want the application, we want the data, we want the decision making, all based in Australia.”

Bringing big tech into the country would make the job much easier, he said, and not just by allowing the army to protect and maintain its datacentres.

The Office of AI, set up in the prime minister’s department, said bringing firms under Australian law would make it easier for local law enforcement to combat threats on the platforms.

Tight conditions on access could also materially improve Australia’s chances of using and defending itself with the best AI tools in the world, the inquiry heard.

“We will get more assured access, earlier access, more detailed technical access, and better integration with technical experts at the frontier,” Bradshaw said.

These would be assured by strict requirements on any top developers looking to train models in Australia, such as demanding government oversight and early access to advanced models, she suggested.

The government is already planning to set the rules for companies that come here. It is consulting on standards that would force AI companies to report issues and breaches and potentially reserve some computational power for local research.

Large datacentres will have to engage with communities, build away from schools and homes, and underwrite new renewables in most states.

Another pillar of the standards – copyright law – is yet to be settled, with AI developers refusing to train models here without law reform.

A proposal to give the companies access to everything Australians create online by default sparked a wave of backlash from creatives, who say the companies could pay for local licensing deals to access Australian content.

But Jenna Priestly, the assistant secretary at the attorney general’s department, on Friday confirmed looser copyright laws would also affect AI access to foreign-made content distributed in Australia.

She said the companies wanted to train models on “maybe billions” of pieces of information and claimed it was practically “impossible” to make deals with every rights holder.

“As Australia’s copyright framework protects not only copyright material that’s Australian in origin, but worldwide, I think it is a fairly large number that [companies] would need to go and strike deals with,” Priestly said.

The Greens senator David Shoebridge, who is among those fighting calls for copyright reform and demanding a pause on AI development, on Friday said Labor had refused him a seat on the inquiry committee.

Labor ministers have spent the week meeting with OpenAI’s vice-president, and Anthropic’s special envoy Jeff Bleich, who this week suggested Australia had just months to bring in effective regulation.

The attorney general’s department told Friday’s hearing the shape and timing of any copyright reform was yet to be decided. But the prime minister’s department said Anthony Albanese wanted draft laws on the broader AI standards by the end of 2026.

Australia’s chance for influence on and special access to the models could be at risk by a delay, Bradshaw said.

“Decisions around training are a matter of urgency,” she said. “I think it is inevitable that those providers will look at other places to locate.”

australia.title: ‘We have something that will kill Elliott’: Icac questions former Labor councillor over message
australia.snippet: Sharangan Maheswaran denies message he received about NSW minister was related to work for fugitive property developer Follow our Austral...
australia.content:
A former Labor councillor says he had a “common interest” with a conservative Liberal operative, but denied that a message he received about damaging the reputation of NSW Liberal minister David Elliott was related to political work for a fugitive property developer, an inquiry has heard.

Sharangan Maheswaran told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that a message sent to him by lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood claiming “We have something that will kill Elliott” did not relate to work by Greenwood’s company Beckington for Jean Nassif.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Maheswaran, who is no longer a councillor, was a lawyer to property developer Nassif and became an executive at his company, Toplace, in September 2020.

Icac is examining whether Liberal figures Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis anticipated receiving $2m in prohibited donations from Nassif in exchange for political outcomes, including damage to the career of former NSW Liberal minister and centre-right faction member David Elliott, who had opposed Toplace developments. Greenwood, Perrottet and Nassif have denied that Nassif paid for political outcomes.

On Friday, Dwyer took Maheswaran to a message Greenwood wrote to him in February 2020 in which he said: “We have something that will kill Elliot.”

Maheswaran replied: “Your ears must be ringing. I just picked up the phone to let you know that I’ve got something decent, and the SMH [Sydney Morning Herald] is going to fire up re [centre-right Liberal MP Alex] Hawke this week off the back of an ALP bill to ban developers.”

Dwyer put it to Maheswaran that the messages showed he shared “a common interest with Beckington in terms of damaging the reputation of David Elliott”.

Maheswaran said he “had a common interest with Mr Greenwood in relation to the Hawke faction of the Liberal party”, but rejected the suggestion the messages related to work by Beckington for Nassif.

When asked if Nassif had told him that Elliott had objected to Toplace proposals, Maheswaran said “this is a new invention by Mr Nassif”.

Dwyer asked him if he “seriously contend[ed] to the commission that Jean Nassif never told you that David Elliott was objecting to his proposals”, asking if Maheswaran was suggesting that Nassif had lied to the commission.

Maheswaran said: “His complaint, up to 2025, as I understood it, was that Mr Elliott was backgrounding against him to the media and to various public officials and government officials, but it wasn’t specifically related to any planning process.”

Asked again if Nassif had lied, Maheswaran said “absolutely”. He was shown a draft statutory declaration he sent to a lawyer in 2022 in which he wrote that Nassif had spoken to Elliott about his opposition to a Toplace developments.

Dwyer put it to Maheswaran that he was “happy to assist him [Nassif] with the political outcome he was seeking, which was to get rid of Mr Elliott”.

“I don’t think that was an objective that Mr Nassif was seeking at that point in time,” he responded.

The inquiry heard that Maheswaran came to know Nassif through his daughter Ashlyn Nassif, who was sentenced to a six-month community corrections order earlier this month after pleading guilty to providing false or misleading information to obtain a $150m construction loan from Westpac.

Maheswaran said he was subcontracted to do work for Toplace through Ashlyn Nassif and her sister Evelyn Helou’s law firm EA Legal in late 2019, through another company, Anwalt Pty Ltd.

But he took issue with Dwyer’s suggestion that he and Anwalt were one and the same.

He said: “That’s nonsensical from a corporation’s perspective, from a commercial perspective, from any sort of understanding of contractual law, I’m sorry, Dr Dwyer, I’m speaking in terms of as I understand the world.”

“No problem,” replied Dwyer. Under questioning, Maheswaran accepted that he was the only shareholder and employee of Anwalt at the time.

Dwyer said: “So the only person doing any actual work was you, correct?”

“At that point in time, yes,” said Maheswaran.

Maheswaran told the commission he was paid $1.4m by Toplace between 2020 and 2023, but said he had not disclosed that he was a close associate of a property developer when he nominated for council in 2021, which Dwyer said was required by law.

Icac is investigating whether Maheswaran and fellow Labor Strathfield councillor Karen Pensabene engaged in conduct towards former mayor Matthew Blackmore in a way “that involves the dishonest or partial exercise of their official functions and/or a breach of public trust, including conduct which could involve blackmail” and possible breaches of the Surveillance Devices Act.

When Icac announced its public hearings, Maheswaran told Guardian Australia: “I have every confidence that my actions will be regarded by the public and by any fair tribunal to be lawful and entirely in the public interest.”

On Friday, the inquiry heard that Pensabene had been excused from her summons for medical reasons.

The inquiry continues.

australia.title: Labor visa overstayer detention centre plan branded a ‘Donald Trump twist’ on immigration
australia.snippet: Australian Greens senator compares government’s policy to ICE as Tony Burke calls it a ‘ridiculous claim’ Get our new political email , f...
australia.content:
The federal government’s move to reopen detention centres for visa overstayers, overseen by compliance officers, has drawn comparison from the Greens and advocates to Donald Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown in the United States.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, was careful to downplay any similarities when he announced the federal government’s immigration plan on Thursday, which includes reducing the roughly 77,000 unlawful non-citizens in Australia.

He told the National Press Club the policy was returning to a “routine process” that existed before 2015, whereby overstayers were brought into detention centres if their visas lapsed prior to securing flights home.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“This is not the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries,” Burke said.

Burke said 100 new compliance officers would be hired to round up overstayers, and an additional 250 beds would be freed, as well as potentially repurposing a 100-bed quarantine facility in Victoria. He said most people would be placed in detention for a matter of weeks, and encouraged to leave of their own accord.

Greens immigration spokesperson, David Shoebridge, said Labor should make visa processes and appeals faster rather than focusing on net migration figures.

“This is where Labor has sunk to, reheating Tony Abbott’s immigration attacks, with a 2026 Donald Trump twist,” he said.

“Labor’s new immigration jails will be run by the same exploitative US private prison multinational that is already abusing people’s rights in immigration detention here.

“If the minister doesn’t want these policies to be compared to ICE, he should not behave like ICE.”

In 2025, the US private prison company Management and Training Corporation won a $2.3bn contract to run onshore detention in Australia under its local subsidiary Secure Journeys, despite serious concerns about MTC’s track record. MTC is one of a handful of private prison operators running ICE detention facilities.

Burke told Guardian Australia Shoebridge was making a “ridiculous claim” by comparing Labor’s policy to the Trump administration’s immigration stance.

“The Green party knows it isn’t true,” he said. “We are simply going back to what Australia had done for decades until mandatory cancellation started, which was to have around 250 beds used when someone no longer had a visa but was refusing to leave.”

The shift occurred under then immigration minister, Peter Dutton, who introduced mandatory visa cancellations for criminal offenders in 2014, which rapidly filled detention centres and saw the department quietly pivot to issuing short-term bridging visas for low-risk overstayers to manage voluntary departures.

Ramping up removals forms part of Labor’s plan to bring net overseas migration down from 292,100 to meet budget forecasts of 245,000 in 2026-27 and 225,000 each year thereafter.

The former head of the Australian Human Rights Commission, Dr Gillian Triggs, told AAP that Australia’s pre-2015 migration detention regime put children in a “horrific pipeline”, with hundreds held in detention without education, most of whom were “severely mentally and physically ill”.

In 2023, a landmark high court decision outlawed indefinite detention without reasonable prospect of being returned to one’s own country, but it’s unclear how that might apply to this change.

The CEO of the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre, Kon Karapanagiotidis, said the federal government had demonstrated “the right to seek asylum and the right to work while seeking safety remain in danger”.

“Minister Burke went to great lengths to reassure Australians this would not look like Donald Trump’s immigration raids,” he said. “But look at what is actually being planned … This will double Australia’s immigration detention regime.

“We will not stand by while migrants and refugees are used as political punching bags.”

Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the immigration department, downplayed the ICE comparisons, pointing out that up until 2015, compliance officers wore “shirts and a tie”, not military gear and were unarmed.

“They operated completely differently,” he said. “They did not enter any premises of any employer without the permission of the employer or a warrant.”

Rizvi said one of the “biggest functions” of the compliance team was educating employers about how to check the working rights of foreign employees, which he said “all appears to have stopped”.

“Given that this cohort is at record levels and grows by around 1,000 per month, what should the government do about a cohort with no remaining right to be in Australia, noting that this cohort will be highly vulnerable to exploitation and live in the shadows of society?” he said.

The legal director at the Human Rights Law Centre, Sanmati Verma, said the federal government should invest in protection for undocumented migrants who had been exploited at work rather than “needlessly expanding the punitive immigration detention network”.

“Rounding up undocumented migrants and locking them in detention is a profoundly anti-worker proposal that undermines the Albanese Government’s commitment to stamping out modern slavery,” she said.

With Australian Associated Press

world.title: British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi rescued by police after shootout
world.snippet: Four of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week A British woman kid...
world.content:
A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.

Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.

Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.

A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.

Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.

Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”

Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.

The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank.

In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.

“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”

Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.

Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outlet Nyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”

Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.

Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.

world.title: Louisiana firefighters find feline native to sub-Saharan Africa while responding to house fire
world.snippet: The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility Louisiana firefighters...
world.content:
Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, and an animal welfare agency is now seeking to place the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.

Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.

A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday.

The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat.

Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands.

Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey.

Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said.

They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility.

JPaws’ statement said the agency would explore having the serval held temporarily at New Orleans’ Audubon zoo. A zoo spokesperson, however, said the institution did not plan to take the serval in and understood JPaws was looking into another arrangement, the details of which were not immediately available on Thursday.

The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boom driven in part by social media content creators showing them in videos online.

Cases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America.

That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati area captured an African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine.

In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated in heartbreak after a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported.

And the news outlet People reported on authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June.

The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.

world.title: ‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writers
world.snippet: More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech...
world.content:
More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.

Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter organised by PEN International and dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.

It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak.

“The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.”

Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali. Six of the writers were profiled in the Guardian in 2015.

The letter, signed by 188 writers in total, calls for “immediate, verified proof of life for all arbitrarily detained Eritrean writers and critics”.

Other signatories include Andrei Kurkov, Anthony Doerr, Chloe Aridjis, Lauren Groff, Lemn Sissay, Maaza Mengiste, Madeleine Thien, Margaret Busby, Max Porter, Philippe Sands, Preti Taneja, Tice Cin and Viv Groskop.

“Mr President, Eritrea’s future must be built with its brightest minds, not based on their suppression,” the letter adds. “No writer or journalist should be disappeared for peacefully expressing their views.”

Eritrea operates as a repressive dictatorship under Afwerki, with no national elections held since independence in 1993.

“We remain in solidarity with our missing colleagues, and we will not cease our efforts until they are free,” the letter concludes.

Earlier this year, PEN International launched a petition, open to the public, which also calls for proof of life.

“Twenty-five years is an unbearable length of time for any family to live without knowing whether a loved one is alive,”, said Burhan Sönmez, president of PEN International. “These writers have not disappeared from our memory. We will continue to speak their names, and we will continue to demand the truth about what happened to them.”

world.title: Almost 50 dead in Nigeria after drinking alcohol suspected to contain methanol
world.snippet: Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated At least 4...
world.content:
At least 48 people have died and about 100 others are receiving treatment in southern Nigeria after consuming a locally brewed alcoholic concoction suspected to contain methanol, officials said on Thursday.

Banji Ajaka, Ondo state’s commissioner for health, said the cases had been reported in the Odigbo and Irele local government areas. A total of 182 people are believed to have been affected and some are being treated in the hospital, he said.

“I took like two shots and I went out on Friday. On Saturday, I noticed that I could not see,” 32-year-old Sola Adebayo told the local TVC News channel from a hospital bed.

Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated.

“This thing happened rapidly. Once they consume, depending on the quantity, the kidneys will pack up, the eyes will go, the brain will be damaged,” Ajaka told The Associated Press, speaking about the drink.

Ondo state police spokesperson Abayomi Jimoh said in a statement that 15 people were arrested in connection with the incident, including one allegedly “involved in the production of substances suspected to contain methanol and is currently assisting the police with investigations.”

Locals told the AP they suspected a popular herbal drink with high alcohol content, known as “Monkey Tail,” was mixed with methanol, causing the deaths.

A trader who sells the concoction in Odigbo, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of being arrested, told the AP there are two versions of Monkey Tail: an original, safe version, and another version which is unsafe.

Local media reports said the first death was reported nearly two weeks ago.

Nigeria’s National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control is now enforcing a nationwide ban on alcohol in sachets and small plastic containers, which it said are easily accessible to children and young people.

world.title: ‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journey
world.snippet: As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own ter...
world.content:
It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah.

But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own.

From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record.

The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012.

Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become.

“Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.”

The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings.

Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates.

Only 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival.

But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whose ancient migration routes are increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes.

“These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape.

“If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says.

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.
